title: Twice as long, half as wide
hook: Double a wire's length and halve its width. Does its resistance double, or worse?

knows: resistance in ohms: more resistance, less current
doesNotKnow: R = rho L / A for a uniform wire
that cross-section area goes with the diameter squared

misconception: Only a wire's length matters, or making it thinner changes its resistance only a little.
objective: The learner can explain that resistance grows with length and with one over the cross-section area, and area goes as diameter squared, so twice as long and half as wide is 2 x 4 = 8 times the resistance.

claims.text: For a uniform wire of one metal at one temperature, resistance is proportional to its length and inversely proportional to its cross-section area: R = ρL/A.
claims.source: Pouillet's law; OpenStax University Physics Vol. 2, section 9.4 Resistivity and Resistance (R = rho L / A).

claims.text: Cross-section area goes with the diameter squared, so half the diameter leaves a quarter of the area and four times the resistance.
If a 1 m, 1 mm wire has 1.0 Ω, the same metal at 2 m and 0.5 mm has 8.0 Ω; the stage's range runs from 0.5 Ω to 48 Ω.
claims.source: R = 1.0 x L / d^2 (L in m, d in mm): 2 / 0.25 = 8.0; minimum 0.5 / 1 = 0.5, maximum 3 / 0.0625 = 48 (artifacts/scratch/w4phys/check.mjs table).

claims.text: The 1.0 Ω reference wire is illustrative; a copper wire 1 m long and 1 mm across is about 0.02 Ω.
claims.source: Copper resistivity 1.68e-8 ohm m at 20 C (CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, Electrical Resistivity of Pure Metals: 1.678e-8 at 293 K): 1.68e-8 x 1 / (pi x (0.5e-3)^2) = 0.0214 ohm. A 1.0 ohm wire of this size needs rho = 7.9e-7 ohm m, in the range of resistance alloys (nichrome 1.10e-6 would give 1.40 ohm).

claims.text: Model: same metal at the same temperature, uniform wire; the stage exaggerates thickness compared with length.
claims.source: Stated on stage ('Same metal', 'Thickness exaggerated') and in the reveal. Resistivity rises with temperature, so a wire that heats up departs from these numbers.

recall.question: You swap a wire for one of the same metal and length but twice the diameter. Its resistance becomes…
recall.why: Twice the diameter gives four times the cross-section area (area goes as diameter squared), so a quarter of the resistance.
